entry.title: TokMem: packing a whole procedure into a single token

link.title: TokMem: packing a whole procedure into a single token

entry.content:
If you use a language model for anything repetitive, you’ve probably built up a little collection of prompts. The careful instructions for formatting a meeting summary. The system message that makes the model answer like a patient tutor. The five-paragraph specification that turns it into a halfway-decent SQL generator.

Each of those is a procedure — a reusable recipe for getting the model to behave a certain way. And every time you use one, you paste the whole thing back into the context window, and the model re-reads it token by token before doing anything useful. The recipe never gets learned; it gets re-explained, over and over.

That re-explaining is the problem TokMem (Wu et al., 2026) sets out to fix.

The cost of explaining yourself every time

Prompting is a wonderfully flexible way to steer a model, but it has stubborn downsides.

First, it doesn’t get cheaper with reuse. A long procedure costs as much on the thousandth query as on the first, and because attention cost grows quadratically with context length, long instructions are expensive. They also eat into the context window the actual input needs.

Second, retrieval doesn’t really fix it. The standard workaround is to store procedures externally and retrieve the relevant one per query, as in RAG-style memory. But what comes back is still text that has to be pasted in and re-read, and the system is only as good as its retriever.

Third, prompts don’t compose cleanly. If a task needs three of your twenty procedures, you concatenate three blocks of instructions and hope they don’t step on each other.

Prompting re-feeds the whole recipe each time; TokMem replaces it with one small token.

One token per procedure

TokMem’s idea is to stop re-explaining and start remembering. Each reusable procedure is compiled into a single trainable token — a memory token — that is added to the model’s vocabulary like any other special token. Training is ordinary next-token prediction on examples of the form query → memory token → response, and only the memory tokens’ embeddings are updated.

Here’s the part that makes it more than prompt tuning: the model chooses the token itself. Memory tokens share their embeddings with the output layer, so after reading a query the model can predict which memory token comes next, just as it predicts a word. Then it generates the response conditioned on that token. For a multi-step task it predicts the next memory token after finishing each segment — parse, then search, then format — and chains procedures without any external controller. If a query doesn’t match any stored procedure, the memory tokens simply don’t win the prediction, and the model answers in plain text.

So one token plays two roles:

  • It’s an index — selecting it says which procedure applies.
  • It’s a control signal — once in context, it steers generation toward that behavior.

And because it’s always one token, the overhead is constant, no matter how long or intricate the original instructions were.

One memory token, two jobs: pick the procedure, then steer the generation.

Keeping the model frozen

The design choice I find most satisfying: the backbone language model doesn’t change. All the procedural knowledge lives in the memory tokens, not in the model’s weights. That separation buys two things:

  • You can keep adding procedures. Training a new memory token doesn’t touch existing ones, so knowledge isn’t overwritten the way it is when you keep fine-tuning shared weights.
  • No retraining the model. Each procedure is a tiny, isolated thing you train on its own, while the expensive backbone stays put.

Isolation alone isn’t quite enough, though. Newly trained tokens tend to end up with larger norms than older ones, and since routing is a softmax over memory tokens, the new ones can crowd out the old regardless of relevance. A one-line fix — rescaling each new token to the average norm of the existing bank — keeps routing balanced. With it, old procedures show only mild declines as new ones arrive. Without it, smaller models noticeably forget.

(One caveat for honesty: in the multi-step tool-use setting, we first give the backbone a short one-time LoRA adaptation on a separate set of tools, so it learns the format of interleaving memory tokens with responses. That adaptation is merged in, and the backbone is frozen again before any of the evaluated procedures are learned.)

How well does it work?

We tested two settings on Qwen 2.5 and Llama models from 0.5B to 8B parameters.

Atomic recall. Each of 1,000 Super-Natural Instructions tasks is its own procedure, and tasks arrive one after another, the way memories accumulate in practice. The key question is whether the model picks the right memory token. At 1,000 tasks, TokMem’s routing accuracy stays above 94% even on the 0.5B model, while the Sentence-BERT retriever used for RAG drops below 80%. That shows up in output quality: on Llama 3.1 8B, TokMem averages 67.0 ROUGE-L, against 50.9 for RAG and 64.7 for LoRA fine-tuning. RAG starts strong but degrades steadily as the library grows; fine-tuning forgets; replay buffers help but still fall short. TokMem is also data-efficient: it beats LoRA at every training-set size we tried, down to 10 examples per task.

Compositional recall. Here each of 50 tools from the APIGen function-calling dataset is a procedure, and each query needs up to four tool calls in sequence. On Llama 3.1 8B, TokMem trains 0.2M parameters versus LoRA’s 3.41M — about 17× fewer — and still edges it out, with 99.1 vs. 98.1 F1 on picking the right tools and 89.3 vs. 87.6 on generating the right arguments. In-context examples and RAG lag far behind on both. TokMem also handles queries with more tool calls than it saw during training.

A detail that matters: where the token goes

Classic prompt tuning puts its learned vectors before the input. TokMem puts the memory token after the query: query, then memory, then response. To isolate the effect of placement, we had both layouts memorize text the models had never seen. With a single token, the after-the-query layout reached 90% of its best perplexity roughly 30% sooner and ended at a lower perplexity. The gap narrows as you add more tokens, which suggests that placement matters most exactly when each token has to carry the most.

Why I think this matters

The mental model I keep coming back to: prompts treat a procedure as something you re-explain; TokMem treats it as something you remember. Once a behavior is worth keeping, it deserves a compact, reusable home — not a paragraph you re-paste into the context window forever.

If the idea keeps scaling, it points toward frozen models backed by growing libraries of single-token skills: modular, cheap to extend, routed by the model itself, and far less prone to the interference that makes continual learning so painful today.

The full details, the experiments, and the math I glossed over here are in the paper.
entry.summary: Compiling each reusable task procedure into a single trainable token, with the language model kept frozen.

entry.title: ULPT: tuning a soft prompt in two dimensions

link.title: ULPT: tuning a soft prompt in two dimensions

entry.content:
Fine-tuning a modern language model is expensive. So a lot of recent work asks a cheaper question: instead of updating billions of weights, can we learn a small “nudge” that steers a frozen model toward our task?

Prompt tuning is one of the tidiest answers. Rather than writing a prompt in words, you prepend a handful of learned vectors — a “soft” prompt — to the input and train only those. The model stays frozen, and you store one small prompt per task instead of a whole model.

But there’s a hidden tax, and that tax is what ULPT (Wu et al., 2026) goes after.

The hidden tax: the model picks your dimension

Each soft-prompt vector has to live in the model’s hidden dimension — the width the model uses internally, often thousands of numbers. A 100-token soft prompt for a model of width d is 100 × d trainable values, and d grows with every generation of models.

You didn’t choose that width; the architecture did. And there’s good evidence that task adaptation doesn’t need it: fine-tuning problems tend to have a low intrinsic dimension. So the parameter budget is set by the model, not by how much steering the task actually needs — and the extra width may even invite overfitting on small datasets.

Vanilla prompt tuning trains the full width; ULPT trains a tiny vector per token and expands it with a frozen random matrix.

The idea: tune small, project up

ULPT’s move is simple: optimize the prompt in a tiny space — as few as two dimensions — and use a fixed random matrix to project it back up to the width the model expects.

For each soft-prompt position you learn a tiny vector z (think 2D). A frozen random matrix up-projects z into a full d-dimensional embedding. The matrix is drawn once and never trained, and you don’t even store it: one random seed regenerates it when the model loads.

There’s one more ingredient, and it turns out to be essential. Learned prompt embeddings vary a lot from one dimension to the next, far more than ordinary word embeddings do. A random projection on its own struggles to match that unevenness. So ULPT adds two learned full-width vectors, a shift and a scale, which are shared across all prompt positions and adjust each output dimension. Without them, training loss stays high; adding the shift fixes most of that, and the scale helps further.

The trainable total is n·r + 2d instead of n·d. On T5-base with 100 prompt tokens and r = 2, that’s 1.7K parameters versus 76.8K — about 98% fewer. (At that setting, most of the 1.7K is actually the shift and scale; the prompt itself is just 200 numbers.)

Only the little vectors (plus a shared shift and scale) are learned; the random projection and the model stay fixed.

Why does a random matrix work?

This is the part that feels like it shouldn’t work. There are two reasons it does, and the paper proves both.

Expressiveness. By the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, a random projection preserves the pairwise distances between a set of points with high probability — and therefore their dot products, which is what attention computes. The dimension you need grows with the logarithm of the number of prompt tokens, not with the model’s width. So a low-dimensional space linked to the model by a random map can capture the relational structure of a full-width prompt.

Optimization. Under standard assumptions, gradient descent through a fixed random projection (with the learned shift and scale) still reaches the global optimum. The frozen matrix doesn’t get in the way of training.

We also checked the obvious alternative: freeze the small vectors and learn the projection. At the same parameter budget, that’s slightly worse, and at the smallest budget it isn’t even possible: learning the projection at r = 2 already brings the total to 3.1K parameters, nearly twice ULPT’s 1.7K.

How well does it work?

Across 21 language-understanding and QA tasks on T5 (GLUE, SuperGLUE, MRQA and four more), the extreme r = 2 setting keeps at least 97% of vanilla prompt tuning’s performance. As far as we know, it’s the first demonstration of prompt tuning working in a two-dimensional parameter space.

Give it a little more room and it pulls ahead. At r = 64 (7.9K parameters), ULPT has the best GLUE and SuperGLUE averages in our comparison (86.0 and 76.8). That puts it ahead of LoRA, which uses 3.8M parameters, and of prompt-tuning variants like DePT and DPT. DPT is the closest relative: it learns the projection matrix instead of freezing it, and at the same rank it uses 7× more parameters and scores lower.

The pattern holds on reasoning with decoder-only models. On GSM8K and MBPP with Llama 3.2 1B and 3B, ULPT at r = 64 uses about 5–7K parameters. That’s about 4× fewer than vanilla prompt tuning and 20–300× fewer than LoRA. It posts the best average on the 1B model and ties the best on 3B, which FourierFT reaches with about 4× more parameters. It also uses the least GPU memory of any method, and because the prompt is computed once and cached, it adds no inference overhead.

Spend your budget on length, not width

There’s a result here I find especially telling. Fix the parameter budget and ask how to spend it. You could buy a short prompt of full-width vectors, or a long prompt of low-dimensional ones. Across T5-small, -base and -large, on both MNLI and Natural Questions, the long low-dimensional prompt wins every time.

Same budget either way — but spending it on more low-dim positions beats fewer full-width ones.

It’s an intuitive trade once you say it out loud. Every extra prompt token is another position the transformer attends over and computes through at every layer. Under a fixed budget, more positions to steer from matters more than more precision per position. Width was the expensive luxury; length is where the budget is better spent — and ULPT’s cheap-per-token design is what makes that length affordable.

The same trade-off shows up in reasoning

I don’t think this is a quirk of prompt tuning. A recent paper, Effective Reasoning Chains Reduce Intrinsic Dimensionality, reaches a strikingly similar place from the reasoning side. It measures a task’s intrinsic dimensionality — the minimum number of model dimensions needed to reach a target accuracy. It finds that effective reasoning strategies push that number down, and that lower intrinsic dimensionality goes with better generalization.

That rhymes with ULPT. There, a prompt with more positions, steered from a tiny space, beats one living in the model’s full width. Here, a better chain of reasoning steps lets the model solve the task with fewer effective dimensions. Different settings, same shape: spread the work over more steps, and what needs to be learned collapses onto a low-dimensional subspace. It hints that “low-dimensional but extended” may be a general property of how these models do useful computation.

Why I think this matters

If you want one model to behave differently for hundreds or thousands of users or tasks, the bottleneck isn’t really inference — it’s storing and managing all those adaptations. ULPT shrinks each one to a few thousand numbers plus a random seed, which makes “one model plus a huge library of cheap task tweaks” practical.

The scope matters, too. We haven’t tested ULPT on models with tens or hundreds of billions of parameters. At that scale I’d expect it to shine at lightweight customization — style, output format, per-user behavior — rather than at teaching the model genuinely new capabilities, which belongs to pre-training.

The deeper takeaway I keep coming back to: the dimensionality of what you tune doesn’t have to match the dimensionality of what the model uses. A fixed random map decouples the two, and once you see that, much of the usual parameter budget turns out to be optional.

The full method, proofs, ablations and per-task numbers are in the paper.
entry.summary: Tuning prompts in an ultra-low-dimensional space and letting a frozen random matrix do the rest, for ~98% fewer trainable parameters.

entry.title: Carrying a soft prompt from one model to another

link.title: Carrying a soft prompt from one model to another

entry.content:
A soft prompt is a short sequence of learned vectors that you prepend to a frozen language model’s input to steer it toward a task. Tuning one is cheap in parameters but not in compute: every gradient step still has to backpropagate through the entire model. For a small model that’s fine. For a large one, it’s exactly the cost you were hoping to avoid.

So here’s the tempting shortcut: tune the prompt on a small, cheap model, then hand it to a large one. Or to next year’s model, so the effort isn’t thrown away when you upgrade.

With a text prompt, that just works — words are words, and you can paste them anywhere. A soft prompt isn’t words. It’s a bundle of raw embedding vectors tuned to one specific model’s internal space, and that’s the portability gap zero-shot continuous prompt transfer (Wu et al., 2024) sets out to close.

Why soft prompts don’t travel

Every model carries its own private map of meaning. Two models might both “understand” language, but the coordinates they use are unrelated — the direction that means “about sports” in one model points somewhere arbitrary in another.

A soft prompt is a few points on one model’s map. Copy those exact coordinates onto a different map and you land somewhere meaningless. How meaningless? Take a prompt tuned on BERT-base and drop it straight into RoBERTa-base — same 768-dimensional width, so the copy is at least possible — and accuracy falls to about 0.1%.

The same coordinates mean different things on different maps, so a direct copy fails.

The idea: describe a prompt by what it’s near

The fix is to stop describing the prompt by its absolute coordinates and describe it by its relationships instead. Take the tokens that both models’ vocabularies share — “river,” “happy,” “run,” and thousands more — and use them as anchors. Then describe each prompt vector not as “these numbers,” but as its cosine similarity to every anchor: this much like river, this much like happy, this much like run…

That list of similarities is the prompt’s relative representation. Because both models know the same anchor words, both can express a vector this way. The relative representation keeps the prompt’s task semantics while discarding the model-specific coordinate frame.

To transfer, run it in reverse on the target model. Start from a random prompt and use gradient descent to make its similarities to the same anchors (measured with the target’s own word embeddings) match the source prompt’s. This search only touches the target’s embedding table — no labeled data, and no backpropagation through the target model.

One practical wrinkle: cosine similarity ignores vector length, so the search can return vectors at the wrong scale for the target. A simple rescale to the mean and spread of the target’s word embeddings fixes that. It barely matters when source and target are the same model, but it matters a lot when they differ.

Encode the prompt as relations to shared words, then find the prompt in the new model with the same relations.

How well does it work?

We tested on factual probing (LAMA): 41 relation types such as place of birth, where the model has to fill in the missing entity. Sources were BERT and RoBERTa; targets also included ALBERT, and we used 8,192 anchors and 5 prompt vectors.

Two reference points make the results readable. On BERT-base, a hand-written prompt scores 30.6%, and a soft prompt tuned directly on BERT-base scores 50.6% — the ceiling for any transfer method. A prompt tuned on RoBERTa-base and transferred with our method, with zero tuning on BERT-base, scores 31.3%. From RoBERTa-base, transferred prompts beat the hand-written ones on four of the five other models. They also beat a trained neural projector between the two embedding spaces in almost every pairing, without having to learn any mapping.

So it isn’t free: transferred prompts still trail prompts tuned on the target itself. But a real share of the task knowledge survives the trip, and you get it without computing a single gradient through the target model. In follow-up experiments the same recipe carried prompts from encoders to GPT-2, and worked on classification too: on SST-2, a prompt moved from RoBERTa-base to RoBERTa-large reaches 84.6%, versus 70.0% for the manual prompt.

A bigger source is a worse source

The finding I found most interesting: large source models transfer worse. Prompts tuned on RoBERTa-large stay under 13% on every other target, even though they work fine on RoBERTa-large itself.

The likely reason is expressiveness. A large, deep model has many equally good soft prompts for the same task, so the one you happen to find carries plenty of model-specific detail on top of the task itself — detail that has no counterpart in another model. Conveniently, the setting we actually care about is small source → large target, which is exactly where transfer works best.

The same reasoning suggests a remedy: if each source adds its own quirks, average over several sources. Matching the relative representations of two source models at once improves transfer. BERT-base plus BERT-large beats BERT-base alone by 2–10 points on the models outside the pair, even though BERT-large is a weak source by itself.

Why I think this matters

Soft prompts are cheap to store but have been awkwardly disposable: retire a model and the prompts tuned for it retire too. Treating a prompt’s meaning as a set of relationships makes that knowledge portable. A small model can act as a “soft prompt engineer” for a large one, producing prompts that can beat hand-written ones without any gradients through the large model.

The broader idea I like is the reframing — meaning as relations, not coordinates. A point is only interpretable relative to a shared frame of reference, and once you choose anchors that both models agree on, a surprising amount of “model-specific” knowledge turns out to be translatable.

The full method, the ablations on anchors and prompt length, and the complete transfer tables are in the paper.
entry.summary: Describing a soft prompt by what it's near, so its task semantics carry across different language models.
